newsitem.title: USA: Clinton proposes $175 billion in highway spending.
newsitem.headline: Clinton proposes $175 billion in highway spending.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Wednesday proposed a six-year, $175 billion program to improve the U.S. surface transportation program, saying it would help build better lives for Americans.

"It does the old fashioned work of investing in America's infrastructure in a very important way, but it also ties those investments to the challenges we face today and tomorrow," Clinton said at a White House rollout of the plan.

Clinton's proposal would increase core highway spending by 30 percent, but also calls for increased spending for auto safety, environmental cleanup, new transportation technology and helping people move from welfare to work.
He said it would "maintain and modernize our transportation system" and "create tens of thousands of jobs for our people."

"The change to reshape America's infrastructure comes along only once every six years. That means that this transportation bill literally will be our bridge to the 21st Century," said Clinton, resurrecting the catchphrase of his re-election campaign.

Clinton said his bill would increase surface transportation funding by $17 billion, or 11 percent, over the $157 billion that Congress authorized in its massive 1991 transportation funding bill, the Intermodal Surface Transportation Efficiency Act.
He said his bill, the National Economic Crossroads Transportation Efficiency Act, or NEXTEA, would give states and localities more flexibility in targeting federal dollars, Clinton said.
And it would expand their opportunities to use innovative financing to leverage U.S. funds, he said.
Clinton said NEXTEA would provide $600 million for innovative technology designed to cut travel time and improve safety.

He said the bill focuses on safety by increasing funds for the National Highway Transportation Safety Administration by 25 percent to $395 million, for highway and truck safety by $2 billion, and for drunk driving prevention by 60 percent.

NEXTEA also would create and expand programs to encourage people to use safety belts and child restraints properly and it would continue research into building safer roads and cars, the White House said.
Clinton said NEXTEA would increase funds to reduce traffic congestion and improve air quality by 30 percent, to $1.3 billion annually.
Funding to support bike paths, pedestrian walkways and other community projects would increase by over 25 percent, he said.
Clinton said the bill provides $600 million to help people leaving welfare to find transportation, such as vanpools, to new jobs.
"This bill is about more than roads and bridges," Clinton said. "It's about those moving from welfare to work and our responsibility to help them get there."
He said the bill also gives states and localities new incentives to train workers for federally-funded technology and construction projects.
